issues.item: Escape Route Planning: always plan an escape route before entering a place
issues.explanation: Escape route planning implies a prominent ongoing external-danger/triggered-threat pattern in public places, but the formulation specifies no active links involving Triggers or Threat, and the rest of the profile is centered on bodily vulnerability and negative beliefs rather than situational danger. This makes the item poorly aligned with the formulation and cross-node content.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: Distrust of others is not impossible after a life-threatening accident, but in this profile it introduces an interpersonal/paranoid theme that is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The remaining items focus on bodily unreliability and permanent damage after an accident, so this item is the least coherent with the trauma-linked appraisal pattern presented.

vignette: Karim, seventy-five, had spent decades shaping stone in a sunlit studio off the coast of Maine, but the life-threatening accident that pulled his car across a fogged highway had fractured something deeper than his collarbone. The sedan had blown a red light, pinning his steering wheel against the guardrail while smoke filled the cabin. For nearly twenty minutes, he lay trapped, his ribs grinding against the column, certain he would suffocate before the county sheriff could cut the glass. That night, he walked out with bruised ribs and a sprained wrist, but the true injury was the sudden, suffocating certainty that his body had been permanently damaged by what happened. He could feel the ghost of every impact, a deep conviction that the metal and glass had irrevocably altered him for the worse. Over the following months, his internal landscape shifted. He had come to believe he could no longer trust his own body, as if the frame that had carried him through decades of carving had suddenly turned unreliable. Every minor ache in his lower back or twinge in his left knee was interpreted as proof of his physical vulnerability, a relentless reminder that his structure was fundamentally compromised. This appraisal did not fade; it festered. When a delivery truck backfired outside his workshop months later, he did not hear a simple sound. He felt the sudden, visceral return of the crushing weight in his chest, and his hands immediately flew to his ribs, checking for structural failure. The memory of the impact did not flash; it lingered in his jaw, a tight, unspoken repetition he performed each time the brakes of a car sounded too loudly against the pavement. Because he viewed his body as irreparably broken and unpredictable, his daily life in the studio had to be entirely restructured. He had come to believe that any exertion could trigger a collapse, so he began constantly checking his body for signs of danger or injury, running his palms over his shoulders, his hips, and his wrists, searching for the familiar solidity that felt increasingly foreign. This vigilance dictated how he worked. He would sit down during the first hour of any project, refusing to lift heavy blocks of marble or stand at the workbench longer than twenty minutes. He avoided physical stress with the precision of a mechanic preventing a breakdown, choosing to sketch on his knees rather than climb the scaffolding he had used for decades. His workshop, once filled with the rhythmic clang of chisels and the smell of wet clay, grew quiet. His hands, which had once shaped stone with confident force, now hovered over tools, trembling at the mere thought of strain. Alongside the checking and the avoidance, a quieter, more persistent question took root. He thought about why the event has happened to him, replaying the screech of tires and the shattering windshield in his mind, searching for a moral explanation that might make the suffering legible. He wondered if it was a punishment for some forgotten failure, or merely a random cruelty that had no reason at all. This meaning-seeking loop ran parallel to his physical precautions, draining his energy and narrowing his world. He stopped accepting commissions, telling his gallery contact that he was taking a long sabbatical, though the truth was that the weight of his own judgments had become too heavy to carry. His widowed status had long been a quiet absence in his life, but now it compounded the isolation, as he could no longer share the space or the silence with anyone. Now, after years of shrinking his world to fit his fears, the isolation has become unbearable. He sits in his studio on Tuesdays and Thursdays, not working, just watching the dust settle on his half-finished figures. He has come to seek help because the silence has grown louder than the crash, and he is afraid that if he does not address the constant dread in his limbs, he will lose the last fragments of the man he used to be. What he hopes for is not a return to his former strength, but a way to quiet the relentless search for meaning and to finally trust his own hands again.
